edits.html: Neonatal herpes without vesicles Timing — seizures, lethargy or apnea in the second or third week of life; vesicles are often absent · Cerebrospinal fluid — normal or mildly low glucose, mildly raised protein, a modest pleocytosis that is mostly lymphocytes, and many red cells · Bacterial meningitis — low glucose and a neutrophil-predominant leukocyte count, often over 1,000/mm3 · Confirm — herpes simplex virus PCR (polymerase chain reaction) of the cerebrospinal fluid · Treat — add intravenous acyclovir to empiric antibiotics without waiting for the PCR · How NBME framed it: no vesicles are given and antibiotics are already begun, so the day of life and the lymphocytic, bloody cerebrospinal fluid identify the virus.

edits.html:
Salient decoyGroup B streptococcus — the antibiotics already begun point toward it, but neonatal bacterial meningitis gives low glucose and a neutrophil-predominant count, often over 1,000/mm3.
Unchecked attributeEscherichia coli — a common cause of neonatal meningitis, but a count of 70 that is mostly lymphocytes, with normal glucose, does not fit a bacterial cause.
True-fact-wrong-slotCytomegalovirus — symptomatic congenital infection shows at birth with periventricular calcifications and hearing loss, not as an acute encephalitis in the second week.
True-fact-wrong-slotToxoplasma gondii — congenital infection shows chorioretinitis, hydrocephalus and diffuse calcifications, not a new encephalitis on day 8.
